newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel denies changed EMU views, sticks by rhetoric.
newsitem.headline: Waigel denies changed EMU views, sticks by rhetoric.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday denied press reports that Bonn had relaxed its hard-line stance on the entry conditions for European monetary union, repeating the rhetoric on the interpretation of the budget criteria that he has used for the last several months.

Responding to reports in the British press which claimed that Waigel -- who has always been a strong proponent of a strict application of the entry test -- had now softened his position, the minister made clear his views were unchanged.

Referring to a requirement that the budget deficits of those nations which wish to join EMU stand at no more than three percent of gross domestic product, Waigel said "three percent is three percent and it will stay that way".
A spokeswoman for the ministry also denied that Waigel had presented a changed view at a meeting of finance ministers this weekend in the Netherlands' seaside resort of Noordwijk.
"The minister's position has not changed in the slightest," she said. "He is sticking to his strict interpretation of the Maastricht qualification criteria for monetary union."
In Basle, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said he had percieved no change in policy in Noordwijk. "When I was in Noordwijk, and I was there, I had not heard of any change."
Two British dailies, the Guardian and the Financial Times, had reported Waigel had shifted his stance, quoting him saying: "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent".
The minister, commenting on Monday in Munich, termed the press reports "unfair in the highest degree".
Countries which wish to meld their currencies in the euro from 1999 must meet economic targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, deficits and public debt levels this year.

Of these, the budget deficit criterion -- which calls for budget deficits to be no more than three percent of GDP except in exceptional circumstances -- is proving for most countries the hardest to meet of the economic entry requirements.

High unemployment and sluggish economic growth has forced countries to revise up their forecasts for spending this year with even Germany -- once Europe's budgetary taskmaster -- now sailing close to the wind with a forecast of 2.9 percent.

Record German unemployment of around 4.7 million in the first two months of the year led many independent economists to brand the official forecast as over-optimistic, leading to market speculation of a fudge in assessing the budget criteria or even a delay in the 1999 launch of the single currency.

Speculation that the changed economic conditions had forced a re-think of Bonn's hardline position was reinforced in February, when Waigel, speaking during a Group of Seven meeting in Berlin, switched his rhetoric from "three means three-point-zero" to "three is three".

He declined to make any explicit clarification of the comment, but independent analysts saw the statement as a signal that a budget level of 3.1 percent, for example, might not in Bonn's view definitively rule out a nation's membership of EMU.

In a measure of the weight of importance attributed to the precise wording of such comments, the finance ministry itself issued a statement making clear that Waigel had said "three is three" and not "3.0 is 3.0" in his comments on Monday.

Germany's repeated insistence on a strict interpretation of the budget rules stems from a need to sell the unknown single currency to an inflation-wary public which is clinging tenaciously to the stable, known quantity of the German mark.
Statements by several high-level politicians -- including Waigel himself -- have stressed the importance of a strict application of the EMU entry test.

Open acknowledgment that a slight overshooting of the three percent level would not necessarily matter could therefore prove a political minefield domestically, as well as taking the pressure off officials to make spending cuts.

But with the participation in EMU of Europe's largest economy seen as critical for the success of the entire project, most independent economists believe a minor overshooting would probably ultimately be tolerated by all concerned.
Germany has already argued successfully that the huge financial strain of German unification gives Bonn a pass card to explain its debt mountain.

And while Waigel has refrained from using this excuse for the deficit position, he made clear in Noordwijk this weekend that Germany would be in the clear on that criterion too without the 1990 merger of the two Germanys.
"In 1989 we had a slight surplus on our budget. We would certainly already meet the criteria now without the burden of the unification costs," he said.
